newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Commodities wind down in holiday mood.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Commodities wind down in holiday mood.

text.p: Commodities put in a lacklustre performance on Thursday as investors wound down ahead of a whopping four-day weekend in Britain.

Most commodities lost any impetus to make gains as trade tapered off in thin volume. Coffee and cocoa were the most dispirited, failing to keep the momentum that saw them rally on Wednesday, and made little progress in soggy trade.

Investors were uninspired by a report from the Association of Coffee Producing Counties late on Wednesday that the supply prospects in the third quarter of 1997 continued to look tight and could be vulnerable to disruptions.
Benchmark May robusta futures slid $12 lower before closing just above par at $1,632.
Cocoa suffered from a bout of profit-taking in the wake of Wednesday's gains and slipped 13 stg to 1,017.

Gold investors were stunned by news that Canadian prospecting company Bre-X Minerals Ltd's gold find at Busang, Indonesia, thought to be one of the world's largest, may contain much less gold than originally thought.
Bullion initially rose on the news but then shrugged it off and settled back down to close at $348.35 an ounce, down from $349.45 on Wednesday.
On the London Metal Exchange, copper bucked the downtrend, and managed to stage a mini-bounce, dragging other base metals higher with it.

Copper sprung up from the key technical level of $2,350 to close at $2,372, up $20. Traders said this helped avert chart breakdowns in aluminium and zinc, which had both been trending lower and threatening to sustain serious losses.
Zinc was pressured on the downside by expectations of Chinese zinc being delivered to Singapore next week and technical selling which kicked-in when the key $1,300 level was breached.
Aluminium closed at $1,642, up $10 while zinc ended $10 higher at $1,295.

The market remains divided as to copper's next move, with some players believing it still needs to do more exploration of its lower range around $2,300 and others expecting further stock falls and tightness will embolden moves above $2,400.
On the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) the quiet holiday mood was not so profound and soybeans and wheat shot up in active trade.

CBOT soybean and soymeal futures opened sharply higher, boosted by surprisingly high weekly export sales while wheat also got a kick from better sales abroad. The CBOT is closed on Friday but opens as usual on Monday.
Meanwhile, Brent crude May oil futures gained 14 cents to $19.43 by 1730 GMT.
